body.text: Form follows physics in Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, where structural load, light, and material permanence meet human experience. Look closely at the spatial geometry and you see how design endures across decades.

Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370 / MAS370) was an international passenger flight from Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia to Beijing Capital International Airport in China. On 8 March 2014, the Boeing 777 operating on the route disappeared from radar with 227 passengers and 12 crew members on board.

Although the cause of its disappearance has not been determined, it has been established that the aircraft was diverted manually but it is unknown by whom or why. It is widely regarded as the greatest mystery in aviation history.
The crew of the aircraft last communicated with air traffic control (ATC) around 38 minutes after takeoff while flying over the South China Sea.

The aircraft was lost from ATC's secondary surveillance radar screens minutes later, but was tracked by the Malaysian military's primary radar system for another hour as it manually deviated westward from its planned flight path. It left radar range 200 nautical miles (370 km, 230 mi) west-northwest of Penang Island in northwestern Peninsular Malaysia.

Relying mostly on the analysis of data from the Inmarsat satellite with which the aircraft last communicated, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) initially proposed that a hypoxia event was the most likely cause given the available evidence, although no consensus has been reached among investigators concerning this theory.

At various stages of the investigation, possible hijacking scenarios were considered, including crew involvement, and suspicion of the aircraft's cargo manifest. Many disappearance theories regarding the flight have also been reported by the media.

With all 227 passengers and 12 crew aboard presumed dead, the disappearance of Flight 370 was the deadliest incident involving a Boeing 777, the deadliest of 2014, and the deadliest in Malaysia Airlines' history until it was surpassed in all three regards by Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 on 17 July 2014.

The search for the missing aircraft became the most expensive search in aviation history at US$135, 160 million. It focused initially on the South China Sea and Andaman Sea, before a novel analysis of the aircraft's automated communications with an Inmarsat satellite indicated that the aircraft had travelled far southward over the southern Indian Ocean.
Several pieces of debris washed ashore in the western Indian Ocean during 2015 and 2016, many of these were confirmed to have originated from Flight 370.

After a three-year search across 120,000 km2 (46,000 sq mi) of ocean failed to locate the aircraft, the Joint Agency Coordination Centre heading the operation suspended its activities in January 2017. A second search launched in January 2018 by private contractor Ocean Infinity also ended without success after six months.
The Malaysian Ministry of Transport's final report from July 2018 was inconclusive.

In the absence of a definitive cause of disappearance, air transport industry safety recommendations and regulations citing Flight 370 have been implemented to prevent a repetition of the circumstances associated with the loss.

These include increased battery life on underwater locator beacons, lengthening of recording times on flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders, and new standards for aircraft position reporting over open ocean.
Background
Aircraft

Flight 370 was operated by a Boeing 777-2H6ER, serial number 28420, registered as 9M-MRO. The aircraft was delivered new to Malaysia Airlines on 31 May 2002. It was powered by two Rolls-Royce Trent 892 engines and configured to carry 282 passengers in total capacity.

6 hours and 7,526 cycles (takeoffs and landings) in service and had not previously been involved in any major incidents, though a minor incident while taxiing at Shanghai Pudong International Airport in August 2012 resulted in a broken wing tip. Its last maintenance "A check" was carried out on 23 February 2014.

The aircraft was in compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives for the airframe and engines. Replenishment of the crew member oxygen system (a routine maintenance task) was performed on 7 March 2014, an examination of this procedure found nothing unusual.

In a 2024 story published without attribution or information about the source, The Standard reported that ten years after MH370's disappearance, "leaked documents" showed that MH370 was given supplemental fuel and crew member oxygen supplies just before takeoff. Passenger oxygen systems can generate about 12 to 15 minutes of supplemental oxygen.
Crew oxygen, which is a separate system, allows for several hours of use.
The Boeing 777 was introduced in 1994 and has an excellent safety record. Since its first commercial flight in June 1995, the type has suffered only six other hull losses.
Crew and passengers

The aircraft was carrying 12 Malaysian crew members and 227 passengers from 14 different nations. On the day of the disappearance, Malaysia Airlines released the names and nationalities of the crew and passengers, based on the flight manifest. The passenger list was later modified to include two Iranian passengers travelling on stolen passports.

The pilot in command was 52-year-old Captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah from Penang. He joined Malaysia Airlines as a cadet pilot in 1981, and after training and receiving his commercial pilot's license, he became a second officer with the airline in 1983.

He was promoted to captain of the Boeing 737-400 in 1991, captain of the Airbus A330-300 in 1996, and captain of the Boeing 777-200 in 1998. He had been a type-rating instructor and a type-rating examiner since 2007. Zaharie had a total of 18,365 hours of flying experience.

The co-pilot was 26-year-old First Officer Fariq Abdul Hamid. He joined Malaysia Airlines as a cadet pilot in 2007, after becoming a second officer of the Boeing 737, 400, he was promoted to first officer of the Boeing 737, 400 in 2010 and then transitioned to the Airbus A330-300 in 2012.

In November 2013, he began training as first officer of the Boeing 777, 200 aircraft. Flight 370 was his final training flight, and he was scheduled to be examined on his next flight. Fariq had accumulated 2,763 hours of flying experience.

Of the 227 passengers, 153 were Chinese citizens, including a group of 19 artists with six family members and four staff returning from a calligraphy exhibition of their work in Kuala Lumpur. There were 38 Malaysian passengers with the remaining passengers being from 12 other countries.
Twenty passengers, 12 of whom were from Malaysia and eight from China, were employees of Freescale Semiconductor.
Flight

Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370/MAS370) was an International passenger flight that departed Kuala Lumpur International Airport at 00:42 (UTC+08:00) on 8 March 2014, heading to Beijing Capital International Airport, carrying 227 passengers and 12 crew members.
The aircraft climbed to its assigned cruising altitude of approximately 35,000 feet (10,700 m) and proceeded towards the waypoint IGARI over the South China Sea.

At 01:21:13, shortly passing IGARI, the aircraft disappeared from secondary surveillance radar, which relies on signals from the aircraft's transponder, and was manually flown through a sharp sustained left turn lasting approximately 2 minutes and 10 seconds.
Investigators concluded that the turn was performed with the autopilot off, as simulator trials could not recreate the manoeuvre within that time using autopilot.

Malaysian military primary radar continued to track the aircraft as it turned back across the Malay Peninsula, passed south of Penang Island and headed northwest along the Strait of Malacca. The final military radar detection was at 02:22:12, beyond waypoint MEKAR. The military identified the aircraft as friendly and did not intercept it.

At 01:38, Ho Chi Minh controllers contacted Kuala Lumpur to report that they had not established communication with Flight 370. Later enquiries were complicated by information from Malaysia Airlines placing the aircraft in Cambodian airspace. At 03:30, the airline explained that its reported positions were projections rather than confirmed locations.
Kuala Lumpur's Aeronautical Rescue Coordination Centre was activated at 05:30, while the aircraft was still airborne.

At 07:24, Malaysia Airlines announced that contact with Flight 370 had been lost and that search-and-rescue operations had begun. Its initial statement initially gave the time of lost contact as 02:40, this was later corrected to 01:21.
